questions.question: In a star schema, what does a fact table contain?
options: Descriptive attributes such as customer name and city
Numeric measures of business events plus foreign keys to the dimensions
Only the primary keys of the source systems
Aggregated reports ready for dashboards
questions.explanation: Facts record events (a sale, a sensor reading) with their measures (amount, quantity, value) and keys to the dimensions that describe them (date, product, customer). Dimensions hold the descriptive attributes.

questions.question: What is the first thing to decide when designing a fact table?
options: Its grain: exactly what one row represents
The BI tool that will read it
Which columns to index
The partitioning scheme
questions.explanation: The grain ("one row per order line", "one row per device per minute") determines which dimensions and measures make sense. Mixing grains in one table leads to double counting.

questions.question: A customer moves from Paris to Lyon and you must keep reporting past sales under Paris. Which technique?
options: SCD Type 1: overwrite the city
SCD Type 2: add a new row with validity dates and a current flag
Delete the customer and recreate it
Store the city in the fact table only
questions.explanation: Type 2 keeps history by versioning the dimension row (`valid_from`, `valid_to`, `is_current`). Old facts keep pointing to the Paris version, new facts to the Lyon version. Type 1 overwrites and loses history.

questions.question: Why use a surrogate key in a dimension instead of the source system's natural key? Select all that apply.
options: It allows several versions of the same entity (SCD Type 2)
It insulates the warehouse from changes or reuse of source keys
It guarantees the quality of the dimension's attributes
It is required to partition the table
questions.explanation: With SCD2 the same customer has several rows, so the natural key is no longer unique; the surrogate key identifies each version. It also protects you when a source system reassigns or changes its keys. It says nothing about attribute quality.

questions.question: Why do analytical warehouses (BigQuery, Snowflake, Redshift) store data by column?
options: Analytical queries read a few columns over many rows, and similar values compress well
Columnar storage makes single-row updates faster
It is required by the SQL standard
It avoids the need for a schema
questions.explanation: An aggregation over 3 columns of a 200-column table only reads those 3 columns, and a column of similar values compresses far better than mixed rows. Row stores remain better for OLTP workloads that read and write whole rows.

questions.question: What do table formats such as Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg or Apache Hudi add on top of Parquet files in object storage?
options: A graphical interface to browse files
ACID transactions, schema enforcement and time travel
Automatic conversion of CSV to JSON
An in-memory cache replacing the files
questions.explanation: They keep a transaction log / metadata layer over the files, so concurrent writes are atomic, schemas are enforced and evolve safely, and you can query a previous version. That is what turns a data lake into a "lakehouse".

questions.question: A table is partitioned by `event_date`. Which query benefits from partition pruning?
options: `WHERE user_id = 42`
`WHERE event_date = '2026-09-01'`
`ORDER BY event_date`
`SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT user_id)`
questions.explanation: Pruning skips whole partitions when the filter is on the partition column. Filtering on another column still scans every partition (unless clustering or indexes help).

questions.question: Why are dimensions usually denormalized in a star schema (vs a snowflake schema)?
options: To save storage space
Fewer joins: queries are simpler for analysts and usually faster
Because normalized tables cannot have primary keys
To prevent any duplicated value
questions.explanation: Putting category, sub-category and brand in one product dimension costs some redundancy but saves joins. A snowflake schema normalizes dimensions into sub-tables, which saves space at the cost of more joins.

questions.question: Order the layers of a medallion architecture, from source to consumption.
steps: Silver: cleaned, typed and deduplicated data
Gold: business-level aggregates and data marts
Dashboards and ML models consume the gold tables
questions.explanation: Keeping the raw bronze layer means you can always rebuild silver and gold after fixing a bug. Each layer adds quality and business meaning.

questions.question: Order the steps of loading a Type 2 slowly changing dimension.
steps: Compare incoming source rows with the current dimension rows to detect changes
Close the current version of changed rows (set `valid_to`, `is_current = false`)
Insert the new version of changed rows (`valid_from = now`, `is_current = true`)
Load the facts, looking up the surrogate key valid at each event's date
questions.explanation: Dimensions are loaded before facts so that every fact can find its key. Looking up the version valid at the event date is what makes historical reports stay correct.
